Part 1: The Prediction Error Problem Imagine you are building a model that predicts house prices (in lakhs) for 5 different houses at a time. You want to compute the overall error of this model — a single number — so that you can try tweaking each individual weight and see how that weight affects the overall error.

Here are the actual prices and your model's predictions: House Actual Predicted 1 1.0 0.9 2 1.1 2.0 3 0.9 0.7 4 0.5 0.3 5 3.0 2.0 Your job: come up with a formula that gives one number representing how wrong the predictions are overall.

Exercise 1.1 — Can We Just Sum the Differences? The simplest idea: for each house, compute , then add them all up. Try it. What number do you get? Does that number accurately reflect how wrong the predictions are? Hint 1 Compute each difference: 0.9 - 1.0 = -0.1, then 2.0 - 1.1 = 0.9, and so on for all five houses. Then add all five numbers. Hint 2 The sum is -0.5. But every single prediction is off by at least 0.1 — so the total error should be positive, not negative. Some positive and negative errors cancelled each other out.

Exercise 1.2 — Fix the Cancellation The problem is clear: positive and negative differences cancel each other out. Think of at least two different mathematical operations that would prevent this cancellation — operations that make every error contribute positively to the total, regardless of whether the prediction was too high or too low. Idea 1: Idea 2: Hint 1 What did you learn in maths class about making negative numbers positive? There are at least two common ways. Hint 2 One approach: take the absolute value of each difference (drop the sign). Another: square each difference (negative times negative gives positive).

What you just invented: You independently arrived at the two most important loss functions in machine learning: Absolute differences → leads to Mean Absolute Error (MAE) Squared differences → leads to Mean Squared Error (MSE) The entire field of regression uses one of these (or a combination). Let's formalise them.

slide_text: Part 3: Why Gradients Matter Remember why we wanted a loss function in the first place? We said: "We need to tweak each individual weight and see how that weight affects the overall error." That is exactly what differentiation does. The gradient of the loss with respect to a parameter tells you: if I nudge this parameter a tiny bit, how much does the loss change? Our training algorithm (gradient descent) depends on this. So our loss function must be differentiable — it must have a well-defined gradient everywhere. Let's check whether our two loss functions qualify.

To keep things simple, let's focus on a single prediction . Define: $[math][math]L_{\text{sq}} = \text{diff}^2[math]L_{\text{abs}} = |\text{diff}|[math]\frac{dL}{d(\text{diff})}$ for each — how the loss changes as the prediction error changes.

Exercise 3.3 — The Problem at Zero You found that the gradient of is +1 when diff 0, and -1 when diff 0. But what is the gradient when exactly ? Is it -1 or +1? Try computing the numerical gradient at diff = 0. Then think about what the graph of looks like at . Is it smooth, or is there something unusual? But is that really the slope? Sketch and look at the shape right at the origin. Hint 2 The graph of has a sharp V-shaped corner at . Coming from the left the slope is -1; from the right it is +1. There is no single tangent line, so the derivative does not exist at that point.

Why this matters: Our training algorithm (gradient descent) works by computing the gradient of the loss and using it to update weights. If the gradient does not exist at some point, the algorithm breaks down. MSE ([math]): Differentiable everywhere. Gradient = [math] — smooth, well-defined, no problems. But the gradient grows without bound for large errors, making training unstable with outliers. MAE ([math]): Not differentiable at diff = 0. The sharp corner means gradient descent has no direction to follow when the prediction is exactly right. So MSE has a problem with large errors, and MAE has a problem at zero error. Can we do better?

You just invented the Huber loss! The standard formulation divides everything by 2 for convenience (so the squared part's gradient is [math] instead of [math]): $[math]$ This is mathematically identical to yours — just scaled by half. It was published by the statistician Peter Huber in 1964 and is built into every modern ML framework: , , 's . You derived it from scratch by asking three questions: How do we measure error without cancellation? → squared / absolute What are the problems with each? → outlier sensitivity / non-differentiability Can we combine them smoothly? → match value and gradient at the boundary → Huber loss

Quick Check 4 — Smooth Transitions The Huber loss uses squared error for small errors and linear error for large ones. What mathematical conditions make the transition smooth at the boundary? A. Only the values need to match B. Only the gradients need to match C. Both values and gradients must match D. Neither needs to match — any transition works

fragments.text: Answer: C. Matching values prevents a jump in the function. Matching gradients prevents a kink (sudden change of slope). You need both for a truly smooth loss that gradient descent can use reliably.
